text: You find the jacket you love in the shop, it looks wonderful on the hanger and then you
put it on and look in the mirror and something is off and you cannot say what it is.
So you tell yourself it is your age or your shoulders or that clothes are just made badly
these days and you buy it anyway and wear it with a little doubt in the back of your
mind.
It is not you, my friend, and it was never your fault because nobody ever taught you
how clothes are supposed to fit.
I spent 50 years at a cutting table and in that time I fitted bankers, bus drivers,
grooms and grandfathers and the same 10 mistakes walked through my door every single week.
Today I am going to count them down and the one at number one is the biggest of the lot
because it costs less than a decent dinner out to fix and almost nobody does it.
So stay with me for that one that.
That my name is Malcolm and I started at 16 sweeping cloth scraps off the floor of a
cutting room in a wool mill town in the north of England.
My old master, Mr. Pettigrew used to say measure it again, lad.
And I have been measuring ever since fit first, fashion second.
That is the whole rule and everything on this list comes back to it.
Right then, let us begin.
Dot number 10 is trousers that are too long.
You know, they look where the hem lands on the shoe and bunches up and folds around the
ankle like it makes the leg look shorter and it makes the trousers look borrowed.
A tailor wants a front of the hem to just touch the top of the shoe.
With one small clean break at the most and a man over 60 looks even sharper with it, a touch
shorter than that.
Shortening a hem is one of the quickest jobs in the shop and it costs very little.
So there is no reason to walk around with cloth piled on your shoes.
Mr. Pettigrew once sent me home to change because my trousers were pulling on my shoes
and he said a tailor who cannot hem his own trousers should hang up his shears.
Number nine is jacket sleeves that are too long.
Stand up straight with your arms hanging down and look at your hands.
If the sleeve swallows your shirt cuff and runs down to your knuckles, it is too long.
A jacket sleeve should stop it about the wrist bone and show roughly half an inch of shirt cuff.
And that little line of white is what tells everyone the jacket was made for you.
A good tailor can shorten most sleeves in a day or two and it changes the whole look of the jacket.
The shoulders never lie, as I always say, but the sleeves give you away just as fast.
And while you have your arms hanging down, have a look at where your trousers are sitting
because that brings us to number eight.
That number eight is trousers that sit too low as the years go by.
The waist changes and the trousers slide down with it until the belt is sitting under the stomach
and the seat hangs loose that creates folds across the front and makes the legs look shorter.
And I say this kindly because I have been there myself.
Bring the waistband up to your natural waist, which is the soft part about level with your belly button
and let the trousers hang straight down from there.
Look for trousers with a higher rise and have the waist fitted so they are held up by the waist
instead of dragged down by the belt and you will stand tall and seat more comfortably.
And if you are wearing black while you are checking all that, we should probably talk about that too.
Number seven is black.
My late wife Evelyn kept the books at the shop and told me honestly when a tie was too loud.
And she always said black next to the face is hard on anyone with silver hair.
She was right as she usually was and she never let me forget it.
Black pulls the color out of the skin and makes the face look tired where a softer shade gives
it warmth. Try a deep navy, a charcoal, a warm brown, a camel or an olive green
and see how your face changes in the mirror.
Keep the black for the evening if you love it.
But in the daytime, hold a navy sweater up to your chin and watch what happens.
Number six is the shirt color that does not fit button, the top button and slide one finger
between the color and your neck.
If you cannot get a finger in, the color is strangling you and if you can fit three,
it is gaping like an open door.
And either way, the ties it's crooked and the whole outfit looks off.
Next change as we get older and a lot of men are still wearing the color size from their 50th
birthday. My granddaughter Poppy, who is 19 and tells me my taste is from the Stone Age,
caught me in one of those the other week and I am sorry to say she was right.
The fix is to get measured again and by the next size that fits you today.
Now, a small favor, my friend.
If this is helping you, a like on the video and a subscribe to the channel
would mean a great deal to an old tailor because it helps other men find these fittings
and it costs you nothing, right? Back to the fitting room.
And number five is a little habit I see on nearly every man who walks in
and it ruins a good jacket in about a week.
So keep listen, asterisk.
Number five is stuffing your jacket pockets.
A wallet in one side, a phone in the other, a set of keys and a handful of receipts on top
and the jacket sags like a fisherman's coat and the pockets stretch out of shape inside a week.
A jacket is cut to hang smooth over the body and every lump you add breaks that line.
Keep the pockets for your hands and a folded handkerchief.
Put your phone and keys in a coat or a bag and slip a slim wallet
into the inside pocket if you really must carry one.
And here's a little tip for you, my friend.
When a jacket is new, the pockets and the back vent are often held shut
with a small cross of thread so the jacket keeps it shaping the shop
and a lot of men wear them stitched like that for years without knowing.
Snip the thread with small scissors, pull it out and the pocket opens the way it was meant to.
Evelyn once spent a whole dinner party staring at a stitched pocket on a customer's jacket
and she wanted to take scissors to it so badly that I had to hold her hand under the table.
Number four is worn down shoes.
A man can have the sharpest jacket in London and if the heels of his shoes are worn down on one side
and the leather is scuff gray, the eye goes straight to the floor and stays there.
A cobbler can fit a new heel for a modest price and a tin of polish and a clean cloth
will do the rest.
Wipe off the dust, rubbing a little polish in small circles and buff it with a soft cloth
until it shines and bobs your uncle a pair of shoes 10 years old looks well cared for.
Poppy keeps telling me I should wear white sneakers with my suit and I told her I would
rather wear my polished shoes. Thank you very much though I will admit a clean pair of plain.
Leather sneakers is perfectly fine with the casual outfit.
Number three is a tie that is the wrong length or width.
The tip of the tie should reach about the middle of your belt buckle.
No higher and no lower.
A tie that stops halfway down the shirt looks like a bib and one that dangles below the belt
looks like a tongue and neither one does you any favors.
The width matters as well and a good rule is that the widest part of the tie should be about
as wide as the lapel of the jacket you are wearing.
Tie it once and look in the mirror and if the tip is short undo it and start again with the knot
tie it a little lower.
I measure twice before I ever cut a piece of cloth and you can do the same with your tie.
Dot number two is the sweater that has seen better days.
After a few winters wool gets little fuzzy balls over the elbows and under the arms
and the cuffs and hem stretch until the whole thing hangs off you like a sack.
Those little balls form where the fibers rub together and they make even a good sweater
look old and tired, lay the sweater flat on a table and run a sweater comb or a fabric
shaver gently over the surface in light strokes and the fuzz comes right off.
Wash wool in cool water with a gentle soap never ring it and dry it flat because hanging
a wet sweater is what stretches it out of shape.
If the cuffs are loose and floppy beyond saving that sweater has done its job and it is time
to let it go and find one with a snug cuff.
Now before we get to number one I need to tell you something that might surprise you
because most men think the answer to all of this is spending more money.
A customer came into the shop once in a very expensive overcoat.
The sort with a price tag that made me whistle and it hung on him like a tent.
The same week a bus driver came in with a plane coat he had bought on sale for a fraction of the
price and when we took in the body and shortened his leaves he looked better than the man in the
expensive one. Price does not fit my friend tailoring a modest jacket altered to your body
would be the costly one hanging loose and that brings me to the one I promised you.
Number one is a jacket straight off the rack that has never been altered.
Nearly every jacket in a shop is made for an average man who does not exist and you are not that
man because nobody is a bespoke suit is cut from scratch to one man's measurements
but for most of us a little alteration does the same job for a fraction of the cost
a good tailor looks at the shoulders first because they are the hardest part to change
so check them before you buy the seam at the top of the sleeve should end right where your
shoulder ends and the collar should lie flat against the back of your neck without a gap
If those two fit a tailor can fix nearly everything else the sleeves can be shortened
the waist taken in so the jacket follows your shape and the length adjusted and jobs like
these often cost somewhere between fifteen and forty dollars depending on where you live
which is less than a decent dinner out button the jacket and look in the mirror if the cloth
pulls into an X across a button or flaps open at the sides tell your tailor and he will know
what to do measure twice buy once and let the tailor have the last word and I promise you will
walk out of that shop CHUFFED. So that is the list my friend hem the trousers shorten the sleeves
lift the waist swap the black for navy and get a tailor to look at that jacket and you have done
most of the work tonight try just one thing and make it this leaves because you can check
them in front of the mirror in about 10 seconds tell me in the comments which of the 10 you have
been guilty of and tell me where you are watching from because I read everyone and Evelyn would
have read them too next time I will show you how a winter coat should fit because that is the one
most men get wrong when the cold comes stay sharp my friend and I'll see you at the next fitting
